blocks.text: A capacitor does not allow direct current to pass, because of the insulating medium between its plates, but alternating current can pass through it. A capacitor is a reactive component: unlike a resistor, it stores energy, in its electric field. When an alternating voltage V is applied across a capacitor C (Fig 17.8 a), it is charged first one way and then the other as the voltage reverses; electrons move to and fro around the circuit, which is the alternating current.

The charge on the capacitor at any instant is q = CV. With V = Vo sin(wt) (17.18), q = C Vo sin(wt), and the current is I = dq/dt = C Vo w cos(wt) = w C Vo sin(wt + pi/2). Writing Io = w C Vo, I = Io sin(wt + pi/2) (17.19). So the current in a capacitor leads the voltage by 90 degrees (pi/2 rad); the voltage lags behind the current (Figs 17.8 b and c).

blocks.title: Capacitive reactance
blocks.text: The opposition offered by a capacitor is its capacitive reactance, XC = Vrms / Irms = Vo / Io. Since Io = w C Vo, XC = 1/(wC) = 1/(2 pi f C), where w = 2 pi f. Its unit is the ohm.
At low frequencies a capacitor has a large reactance and the current is small; at high frequencies its reactance is small and the current through the same capacitor is large.

blocks.alt: Three rows. Resistor: a circuit of an AC source and a resistor R; graphs of V (green) and I (red) rising and falling together; phasors V and I in the same direction; R = V/I. Inductor: a source and a coil L; the current graph is a quarter cycle behind the voltage; phasor I points 90 degrees behind V; XL = wL = 2 pi f L. Capacitor: a source and a capacitor C; the current graph is a quarter cycle ahead; phasor I points 90 degrees ahead of V; XC = 1/wC = 1/(2 pi f C).
blocks.caption: AC through a resistor, an inductor and a capacitor (original diagram after Figs 17.6 to 17.8).
blocks.long_description: A resistor keeps V and I in step. An inductor resists changes in current, so the current falls a quarter cycle behind; a capacitor must be charged by the current before its voltage can rise, so the current runs a quarter cycle ahead.

blocks.title: Do you know?
blocks.text: Nikola Tesla, called the father of alternating currents, was born in 1856 in Austria-Hungary and emigrated to the USA in 1884. He pioneered the generation, transmission and use of alternating current, which can be transmitted over much greater distances than direct current.
